P1:
Roblox is renaming yielding methods to carry an Async suffix. The old names are deprecated aliases that keep working, but new code should use the new names:
- Player:LoadCharacter -> Player:LoadCharacterAsync
- BadgeService:AwardBadge -> BadgeService:AwardBadgeAsync
- MarketplaceService:GetProductInfo -> MarketplaceService:GetProductInfoAsync
- RemoteFunction:InvokeServer -> RemoteFunction:InvokeServerAsync (and InvokeClient -> InvokeClientAsync)
- Instance:WaitForChild: as far as I know it was not renamed. It stays WaitForChild because it is a core idiom, so there is nothing to migrate.
The deprecated names behave the same (no runtime break). Expect Script Analysis deprecation warnings, and expect autocomplete and docs to show only the Async names. Migrate with find/replace, keep pcall around the yielding network calls, and check the API reference for the exact final names before you rely on any of this.
P2:
Server Authority is turned on in Workspace with the authority-mode property (Workspace.AuthorityMode = Server, a beta at first). When it is on, the server is authoritative for physics and character movement and clients predict and roll back. It forces the settings it depends on: StreamingEnabled on, the new physics/fixed-step simulation, and server-authoritative character replication. Client-side network-ownership tricks and SignalBehavior workarounds stop applying.
Gameplay logic the client predicts (movement, abilities, projectiles that touch physics) must be deterministic code shared by client and server: ModuleScripts in ReplicatedStorage, run from RunService's simulation-step callback (RunService:BindToSimulation), not Heartbeat or RenderStepped. That code should read the simulation clock (the fixed-step simulation time passed to and exposed by that callback), not os.clock/tick/time() or the render frame delta. That way the server and a rolled-back client resimulate the same steps and get identical results. Input should come through Input Action System actions so it can be recorded and replayed.
P3:
The switch is a StarterPlayer property that selects whether the default PlayerModule (ControlModule/CameraModule) runs on the Input Action System. It is an enum with Default / Enabled / Disabled (the opt-in and opt-out). Rollout: first an opt-in beta where Default means old behaviour, then Default flips to the IAS-based scripts, then the opt-out is removed and the old ContextActionService-based scripts are retired. Opt out temporarily with Disabled while you fix things.
Code at risk:
- Forked or edited copies of PlayerModule, and code that requires its internals (ControlModule:GetMoveVector, BaseCharacterController, Keyboard/Gamepad/TouchThumbstick modules, ControlModule:Disable/Enable patterns).
- ContextActionService code that unbinds, overrides or relies on the default action names (moveForwardAction, jumpAction, etc.) or on bind priorities against them.
- Scripts that hunt for the TouchGui/TouchControlFrame/JumpButton or reposition the thumbstick by name.
- Code that assumes UserInputService.ModalEnabled or the old touch GUI layout disables controls.
P4: The October 2026 TextChatService update tightened access to raw message text. Messages are filtered and delivered per recipient, so TextChatMessage.Text is the filtered, recipient-appropriate string. Games must not show or store unfiltered text, and must not build their own message pipeline over RemoteEvents. Custom chat UIs have to render messages that come through TextChatService (MessageReceived/OnIncomingMessage, TextChannel:SendAsync) and respect the age and chat-eligibility checks (CanUserChatAsync / CanUsersChatAsync, TextChannel:CanSendMessage gating). Treat Text as read-only display data, and use Metadata / OnIncomingMessage properties for styling instead of rewriting text. Legacy Chat is fully gone. Rollout: announced with an opt-in period, then enabled by default for all experiences, with the legacy behaviour removed a few months later. Test your custom UI under the new setting before enforcement. I am not certain of the exact dates.
P5:
Since 2026, DataStore limits are calculated per experience and scale with audience instead of being a flat per-server allowance.
- Storage: base 100 MB plus 1 MB per lifetime unique user (lifetime users x 1 MB + 100 MB).
- Requests: an experience-wide budget per minute that scales with concurrent users. The classic per-server write budget is 60 + numPlayers x 10 requests/min (Set/Increment/Remove/Update), with similar formulas for Get (60 + 10n), GetSorted (5 + 2n) and List (5 + 2n). There are also per-key limits (about 1 write per 6 seconds per key) and a 4 MB value size cap.
- UpdateAsync counts against both the read (Get) and the write (Set) budgets, because it does a read and a conditional write. If the transform returns nil, nothing is written.
Check DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before bursts, batch per-player data into one key, and back off when the budget is low.
P6:
Roblox's paid random item policy covers anything bought directly with Robux or indirectly (Gems bought with Robux), so the Gem crates count.
Before purchase you must show:
- The odds (probability) of every item or rarity tier in the crate, clearly, in the purchase UI.
- The changed odds while the Luck Potion is active. A paid odds boost must show the boosted probabilities, so players see the real odds they are paying for.
For each player you must check policy:
- Call PolicyService:GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync(player) in a pcall and read ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted. If it is true (some countries), disable buying crates with Robux-bought currency and the paid luck boost for that player, or offer only non-random direct purchases.
- Also respect IsPaidItemTradingAllowed if crate items can be traded.
- Fail closed: if the policy call errors, treat paid random items as restricted.
Enforce all of this on the server, not just in the UI. Mark the experience's monetization in the maturity/compliance questionnaire.
P7:
Roblox Kids and Roblox Select are age-scoped account experiences. Roblox Kids is for the youngest users (under about 9). Roblox Select is a curated mode for the next band of younger users. Both see only a restricted, vetted catalogue of experiences, with chat and social features limited by default.
For an experience to be available to them:
- The creator needs a verified, trusted account (ID or age verification, in good standing, no recent moderation strikes). For groups, the owner is verified.
- The experience needs a completed Maturity & Compliance questionnaire rated Minimal (no violence or fear beyond mild, no romance, no paid random items unless policy-compliant, no unrated or social-hangout content). It must comply with the policies for those ages (PolicyService checks, no external links, no unfiltered UGC or text).
- It is opted in or eligible on the Creator Dashboard and passes Roblox review or curation for Select.
I am not sure of the exact age bands or eligibility thresholds; check the Creator Hub.
P8:
Creator Rewards (launched 2025, replacing Engagement-Based Payouts) pays in Robux, from Roblox, on top of normal sales revenue. It has two parts:
1. Daily engagement rewards: payouts based on the share of time that active spenders (users who spent Robux recently, including Premium members) spend in your experience.
2. Audience expansion rewards: payouts for bringing new users, or lapsed users returning, to Roblox through your experience (for example via shared links).
Payouts are calculated daily and credited after a holding period. Eligible experiences must be public, meet monetization eligibility and follow policy.
DevEx: the standard rate is about $0.0038 per Robux (raised from $0.0035 in 2025), so 100,000 Robux is roughly $380. The 2026 boosted rate for US creators aged 18+ is higher, about $0.0045 per Robux, but I am not certain of that number; check the DevEx page.
G1:
ProcessReceipt rules:
1. Set it exactly once, in one server Script. A later assignment overwrites it.
2. Return PurchaseGranted only after the grant is durably saved. Otherwise return NotProcessedYet; Roblox then retries the receipt on the player's next join or purchase.
3. Be idempotent per receipt.PurchaseId. Record processed PurchaseIds in the player's saved data, in the same UpdateAsync that grants the item, and return Granted if the id is already present.
4. If the player is not in the server (GetPlayerByUserId is nil), return NotProcessedYet. Don't grant into nothing.
5. Wrap DataStore calls in pcall. On any error, return NotProcessedYet. Never let the callback error or yield forever.
6. Look up handlers by ProductId; an unknown product returns NotProcessedYet.
Charged but got nothing: the callback returned Granted before the save succeeded (or ignored a pcall failure), the player left, or the server shut down mid-save, so the receipt was closed with no grant.
Item received twice: the receipt was retried (a NotProcessedYet return, a timeout, or a second server) and the code doesn't dedupe by PurchaseId. A second cause is read-then-SetAsync races.
G2:
Use UpdateAsync whenever the new value depends on the old value or several servers could write the same key: currency changes, purchases, trades, session locks, incrementing stats. SetAsync blindly overwrites, so a stale server (after teleport or rejoin) can roll data back or lose a concurrent change. UpdateAsync reads the latest value and writes atomically; on a conflict it re-runs your transform.
Transform function rules:
- No yielding (no task.wait, no other DataStore calls, no WaitForChild).
- Pure and fast. It may be called more than once, so no side effects (don't grant items or fire remotes inside it).
- Handle nil (first-time player) and validate the old data (version or session lock check).
- Return the new value to write, or nil to cancel the write.
- Return only serializable data (no Instances, no mixed tables, under 4 MB).
- Don't mutate shared upvalue state you rely on outside it.
Wrap the call in pcall and retry with backoff. UpdateAsync uses both read and write budget.
G3:
It is not safe.
1. NaN: typeof(NaN) == "number", and NaN < 0 and NaN > x are both false, so 0/0 passes every check and can corrupt the trade math.
2. Infinity is rejected by the max check, but non-integer values (0.0001, 1e-300) pass, so fractional gold leads to rounding exploits.
3. It is a time-of-check/time-of-use bug. The gold is only checked, not reserved. The player can create many offers, or spend the gold after offering, so the same gold is promised multiple times. The real check must happen again atomically when the trade completes.
4. There is no rate limit or trade-state validation (is there an open trade, is the partner valid).
Fix:
```lua
offerRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, gold)
    if typeof(gold) ~= "number" or gold ~= gold or gold % 1 ~= 0 then return end
    if gold < 0 or gold > player.Gold.Value then return end
    local trade = activeTrades[player]
    if not trade or trade.locked then return end
    trade.offers[player] = gold          -- replace, don't add
end)
-- on completion: re-check both balances, then move gold atomically (escrow)
```
Escrow or deduct the gold on confirm, and verify it again server-side at commit.
G4:
The Animator overwrites Motor6D.Transform every frame. It runs after Heartbeat's predecessor stage. In each frame, animations are stepped during the simulation (PreSimulation) and Transform is set from the active tracks, so anything you write in Heartbeat or before is replaced on the next step, or immediately while a track drives that joint. Transform is meant for animation output.
For procedural offsets on top of animations, write Transform after the Animator has run and before rendering or replication. Use RunService.PreSimulation (formerly Stepped) and compose with the animated value instead of replacing it:
```lua
RunService.PreSimulation:Connect(function()
    motor.Transform = motor.Transform * CFrame.Angles(0, yaw, 0) * CFrame.Angles(pitch, 0, 0)
end)
```
Alternatives: make the idle animation not key that joint, so it doesn't drive it, or use an IKControl.
Edit C0/C1 instead when the offset should be a persistent rest pose rather than a per-frame layer: for example a permanent re-orientation of the joint, or aiming when no animation touches the joint. C0 changes replicate from the server (Transform does not), so on the server-owned turret, C0 is the one other clients will see. Animations are then applied relative to the new C0.
G5:
Each AnimationTrack has a Priority (Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4). For each joint, only tracks with the highest priority among those that animate that joint are used. Lower-priority tracks are ignored on that joint. If equal-priority tracks animate the same joint, they are blended by weight.
The default walk is Movement. If your swing was exported as Core, Idle or Movement, the walk either overrides it or blends with it, so it looks weak or invisible. Fix: set the swing to Action (or higher), in the Animation Editor before export or with track.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action after loading.
Weights: track:Play(fadeTime, weight, speed) or track:AdjustWeight(w, fade). Within one priority level, joint poses are blended in proportion to the tracks' effective weights (WeightCurrent, which ramps during fade-in/out). A track with weight 1 alone fully poses the joint; two equal tracks at weight 1 each contribute 50%. Weight does not let a lower priority beat a higher one. Keyframes that don't key a joint leave that joint free for lower priorities.
G6:
Blender's default unit is the metre, and Roblox imports FBX assuming 1 unit = 1 stud (or reads a cm-based scale), so a 2 m model becomes about 200 studs. The FBX unit scale (Blender metres vs FBX centimetres, a factor of 100) isn't applied the way you expect.
Recommended setup:
- Scene Properties > Units: Unit Scale 0.01, Length Centimeters (or keep metres and fix the scale on export), and model at Roblox scale (1 stud ~ 0.28 m; a character is about 5 studs tall).
- FBX export: Apply Scalings = FBX Units Scale (or "FBX All"), Forward -Z, Up Y, Apply Unit and Apply Transform enabled, export Selected Objects, Mesh plus Armature only. Apply modifiers, triangulate optionally, no leaf bones for rigs.
- Apply all transforms (Ctrl+A, Scale/Rotation) before export.
- In the Studio 3D Importer you can also adjust the scale or unit setting, but fixing it at the source is best. GLB/glTF export (metres) is often simpler.
G7:
Modifiers are non-destructive. Unless the exporter applies them, the .glb contains only the base mesh: the half you modelled, before Mirror, and the unbevelled edges. Roblox never sees Blender modifiers.
Fix: tick Apply Modifiers in the glTF exporter (Include/Mesh > Apply Modifiers), or apply them manually (Ctrl+A > Apply) on a copy before export.
The catch: the glTF exporter cannot apply modifiers on meshes that have shape keys. Shape keys are skipped or the export errors, and many glTF versions simply don't export shape keys when Apply Modifiers is on. Armature modifiers are handled separately for skinning, so applying everything can break rigs. Bevel and Mirror also raise the triangle count (watch the 20k-tri limit per mesh) and can create split normals; check the shading (Auto Smooth / Weighted Normal). The usual answer: apply Mirror and Bevel destructively on a duplicate, keep the original, and keep the armature as a modifier.
G8:
1. Stretching: UDim2.fromScale(0.3, 0.3) is 30% of the width and 30% of the height. On a 16:9 monitor that is one shape; on a tall phone or 4:3 tablet the aspect ratio changes, so the frame is stretched. Fix: add a UIAspectRatioConstraint (AspectRatio = 1 for square, or your design ratio, with DominantAxis set). Or size on one axis (Size = {0.3,0},{0.3,0} plus SizeConstraint = RelativeXX/RelativeYY). Add UISizeConstraint/UITextSizeConstraint for minimum and maximum sizes.
2. Hidden by the notch or top bar: with ScreenGui.IgnoreGuiInset = true, or ScreenInsets = None, your (0,0) corner is under the Roblox top bar buttons and phone notches. Fix: ScreenGui.ScreenInsets = Enum.ScreenInsets.CoreUISafeInsets (avoids the top bar and notch) or DeviceSafeInsets (notch only). Also use ScreenGui.SafeAreaCompatibility, and leave IgnoreGuiInset false for interactive HUD. Put full-bleed decorative backgrounds in a separate ScreenGui with ScreenInsets = None. Use AnchorPoint plus a small offset margin, and test in the Device Emulator with notched devices.
T1:
```lua
local RS = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local Items = require(game.ServerStorage.ItemCatalog) -- [itemId] = {price=number}
local BuyItem = RS.Remotes.BuyItem
local MAX_QTY, COOLDOWN = 99, 0.25
local last = {}

BuyItem.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, itemId, quantity)
    local now = os.clock()
    if last[player] and now - last[player] < COOLDOWN then return end
    last[player] = now

    if typeof(itemId) ~= "string" or #itemId > 50 then return end
    if typeof(quantity) ~= "number" or quantity ~= quantity
        or quantity % 1 ~= 0 or quantity < 1 or quantity > MAX_QTY then return end

    local item = Items[itemId]
    if not item then return end

    local coins = player:FindFirstChild("leaderstats") and player.leaderstats:FindFirstChild("Coins")
    if not coins then return end
    local cost = item.price * quantity
    if coins.Value < cost then return end

    coins.Value -= cost                       -- server-owned balance
    PlayerData.addItem(player, itemId, quantity) -- server inventory
end)

game:GetService("Players").PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(p) last[p] = nil end)
```
Price comes from the server catalogue, never the client. Types, NaN and integers are checked, the request is rate-limited, and the deduct and grant happen with no yield in between.
T2:
```lua
-- key value: {data=..., lock={jobId=, time=}}
local LOCK_TTL = 1800 -- stale lock expiry
function load(player)
    for attempt = 1, 5 do
        local ok, result = pcall(store.UpdateAsync, store, key(player), function(v)
            v = v or {data = defaultData(), lock = nil}
            local l = v.lock
            if l and l.jobId ~= game.JobId and os.time() - l.time < LOCK_TTL then
                return nil -- locked by another server: abort write
            end
            v.lock = {jobId = game.JobId, time = os.time()}
            return v
        end)
        if ok and result and result.lock.jobId == game.JobId then
            sessions[player] = result.data; return true
        end
        task.wait(attempt * 2) -- old server may still be saving
    end
    player:Kick("Data busy, rejoin"); return false
end

function save(player, release)
    local data = sessions[player]; if not data then return end
    pcall(store.UpdateAsync, store, key(player), function(v)
        if not v or not v.lock or v.lock.jobId ~= game.JobId then return nil end
        v.data = data
        v.lock = (not release) and {jobId = game.JobId, time = os.time()} or nil
        return v
    end)
end
-- autosave every 60s with save(p,false) (refreshes lock time)
-- PlayerRemoving: save(p,true); sessions[p]=nil
-- BindToClose: save all with release, wait for completion
```
Key points: only the lock owner may write, so stale servers can't overwrite. The new server waits or retries until the old one releases the lock. Locks expire if a server crashes. Saves use UpdateAsync, never SetAsync. Teleport after the save releases the lock. ProfileStore implements exactly this.

T4:
FireServer automatically sends the firing player as the first argument to OnServerEvent. The client passed LocalPlayer explicitly as well, so the server receives (player, LocalPlayer, 50). amount is then the Player Instance, and amount + 1 errors.
Fix: don't pass the player.
```lua
-- client
remote:FireServer(50)
-- server
remote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, amount)
    if typeof(amount) ~= "number" or amount ~= amount then return end
    print(amount + 1)
end)
```
Always trust the implicit player argument, never a player the client sends. And validate every client argument's type.
T5:
In Studio solo play, the local player can join before your server Script runs, for example when it does yielding work (require, WaitForChild, DataStore calls) before connecting. PlayerAdded has already fired for that player, so your handler never runs for them. On live servers scripts usually load before anyone joins, which hides the race.
Standard fix: connect the event, then loop over the players already in the game.
```lua
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local function onPlayerAdded(player)
    local ls = Instance.new("Folder")
    ls.Name = "leaderstats"
    local coins = Instance.new("IntValue")
    coins.Name = "Coins"
    coins.Parent = ls
    ls.Parent = player
end
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(onPlayerAdded)
for _, p in Players:GetPlayers() do
    task.spawn(onPlayerAdded, p)
end
```
Also connect before any yields at the top of the script.

T8:
RenderFidelity is not a runtime-scriptable property. It is applied when the mesh is loaded or imported. Changing it from a script at runtime does nothing (scripts can't set it; you get an error or no effect), so set it in Studio before publishing. Even Precise doesn't stop distance-based detail reduction entirely:
- Precise disables mesh LOD switching only on the mesh itself. The engine's global quality level (the player's Graphics Quality slider, automatic quality, mobile devices) still lowers detail and draw distance.
- Instance streaming and Model.LevelOfDetail/ModelStreamingMode can replace distant models with low-detail imposters (StreamingMeshDetail). Set the model's LevelOfDetail to Disabled or give hero models ModelStreamingMode = Persistent.
- The asset itself may have been generated with LODs at upload, and textures mip down with distance regardless.
- Very small meshes are culled at distance whatever the fidelity.
Also check that the property was saved on the published copy (packages or meshes inserted at runtime use the default Automatic). Test with Graphics Quality at max. Precise costs performance, so use it only on true hero assets.
